statement: Let $G$ be a path-connected [topological group](c:topological-group) with [loop group](c:loop-group) $LG = \mathrm{Map}(S^1, G)$, and let $M$ be a metrizable, [locally contractible](c:locally-contractible-space) space. Taking sections over the circles $\{m\} \times S^1$ sends [principal bundles](c:principal-bundle) with group $G$ over $M \times S^1$ bijectively, up to isomorphism, to principal $LG$-bundles over $M$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a path-connected [topological group](c:topological-group).
The base $M$ is metrizable and [locally contractible](c:locally-contractible-space), for example a manifold.

conclusion: The map $P \mapsto \Gamma(P)$, with $\Gamma(P)_m$ the sections of $P$ over $\{m\} \times S^1$, is a bijection on isomorphism classes, with inverse $Q \mapsto Q \times_{LG} (S^1 \times G)$.

proofs.name: Bundle of sections along the circles
proofs.slogan: Take the sections of the bundle over each circle to get an LG-bundle, and recover the bundle by evaluating sections.
proofs.scope: The topological version up to isomorphism. Path-connectedness of $G$ makes every $G$-bundle over a circle trivial, and the loop bundle $LP \to LX$ is the case $M = LX$ with $P$ replaced by $\mathrm{ev}^*P$, for a manifold $X$.

roles.why: Path-connectedness makes each restriction $P|_{\{m\}\times S^1}$ trivial, so every section space is a nonempty torsor.
Local contractibility gives contractible neighborhoods $U$ over which the bundle is a pullback from a circle.

steps.slogan: Form the space of sections of $P$ over each circle $\{m\} \times S^1$.
steps.detail: Let $Q_m$ be the set of sections of $P$ over $\{m\} \times S^1$, with the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology). The loop group acts on $Q_m$ by pointwise right multiplication. This [torsor](c:torsor) structure is free and transitive, because two sections of a principal bundle differ by a unique $G$-valued function. The set $Q_m$ is nonempty because $P|_{\{m\}\times S^1}$ is trivial.

steps.slogan: Trivialize the bundle over $U \times S^1$ for a contractible neighborhood $U$.
steps.detail: Take a contractible open $U \ni m$. By [homotopy invariance](c:homotopy-invariance) of bundles over the metrizable, hence paracompact, space $U \times S^1$, $P|_{U \times S^1}$ is isomorphic to the pullback of $P|_{\{m\}\times S^1}$, which is trivial. So $P|_{U\times S^1} \cong U \times S^1 \times G$ and the section spaces over $U$ form $U \times LG$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the section spaces form a principal $LG$-bundle over $M$.
steps.detail: The local trivializations are compatible: the transition maps $U \cap U' \to LG$ are continuous by the exponential law for the compact space $S^1$. So $\Gamma(P) = \bigsqcup_m Q_m \to M$ is a locally trivial principal $LG$-bundle. An isomorphism of $G$-bundles induces an isomorphism of the section bundles.

steps.slogan: Build the inverse by letting $LG$ act on $S^1 \times G$ through evaluation.
steps.detail: For a principal $LG$-bundle $Q \to M$, let $LG$ act on $S^1 \times G$ by $\gamma\cdot(t,g) = (t, \gamma(t)g)$. Put $P_Q = Q \times_{LG} (S^1 \times G)$, an [associated bundle](c:associated-bundle) with $G$ acting on the right of the factor $G$. Where $Q$ is trivial over $U$, $P_Q \cong U \times S^1 \times G$, so $P_Q$ is a principal $G$-bundle over $M \times S^1$.

steps.slogan: Check that the two constructions are inverse to each other.
steps.detail: The map $Q \to \Gamma(P_Q)$, $q \mapsto (t \mapsto [q,t,e])$, is an equivariant map of $LG$-torsors over $M$, hence an isomorphism. The map $P_{\Gamma(P)} \to P$, $[\sigma,t,g] \mapsto \sigma(t)g$, is a morphism of principal $G$-bundles, hence an isomorphism. Both constructions respect isomorphisms, so the isomorphism classes correspond.

source.note: The caloron correspondence of M. K. Murray and D. Stevenson (Higgs fields, bundle gerbes and string structures, Comm. Math. Phys. 243 (2003), 541-555); this is its topological form, with sections over the circles.

concepts.c:associated-bundle: The inverse bundle is the associated bundle with fibre $S^1 \times G$.
concepts.c:compact-open-topology: This topology makes each section space a topological torsor over $LG$.
concepts.c:homotopy-invariance: Homotopy invariance trivializes the bundle over a contractible set times the circle.
concepts.c:locally-contractible-space: Contractible neighborhoods make the bundle a pullback from a circle.
concepts.c:loop-group: The loop group $LG$ is the structure group of the section bundle.
concepts.c:principal-bundle: Both sides of the correspondence are isomorphism classes of principal bundles.
concepts.c:topological-group: The group $G$ and the loop group are topological groups acting on bundle fibres.
concepts.c:torsor: Each section space is a torsor, so equivariant maps of torsors are isomorphisms.

statement: Let $\mathcal I$ be a real [analytic](c:analytic-function) [exterior differential system](c:exterior-differential-system) on a manifold $M$, and let $E \subset T_pM$ be a Kähler-regular integral element of $\mathcal I$. Then a real analytic integral manifold of $\mathcal I$ passes through $p$ with tangent space $E$ at $p$.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ and the [differential ideal](c:differential-ideal) $\mathcal I$ are real analytic, and $\mathcal I$ is closed under exterior differentiation.
The subspace $E \subset T_pM$ is an integral element of $\mathcal I$ that is Kähler-regular.

conclusion: There is a real analytic integral manifold $N$ of $\mathcal I$ with $p \in N$ and $T_pN = E$.

proofs.name: Dimension by dimension with Cauchy-Kovalevskaya
proofs.slogan: Build the integral manifold one dimension at a time, solving a Cauchy-Kovalevskaya system at each step.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, which rests on the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem; the step from dimension $k$ to $k+1$ is the form of the theorem for Kähler-regular integral manifolds. The theorem generalizes the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya and Frobenius theorems.

roles.why: Regularity gives a flag of integral elements whose polar spaces have constant dimension, so each step is a determined system.
Analyticity lets the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem apply, and closure under $d$ makes the rest of the ideal vanish on the solution.

steps.slogan: Choose a flag of regular integral elements that ends at $E$.
steps.detail: Because $E$ is Kähler-regular, there is a flag $0 = E_0 \subset E_1 \subset \dots \subset E_n = E$ of integral elements with $\dim E_k = k$, each regular, so the polar spaces $H(E_k)$ have constant dimension nearby. Set $N_0 = \{p\}$.

steps.slogan: Describe the next integral elements by the polar equations of $E_k$.
steps.detail: The polar space $H(E_k)$ holds the vectors $v$ for which $E_k + \langle v \rangle$ is an integral element. It is cut out by analytic linear equations that vary analytically along $N_k$. Regularity keeps their rank constant, so an analytic submanifold $R_k \supset N_k$ of the right codimension makes the problem determined.

steps.slogan: Write the integral manifold condition as a Cauchy-Kovalevskaya system.
steps.detail: In coordinates adapted to $N_k \subset R_k$, a $(k+1)$-dimensional submanifold $X$ with $N_k \subset X \subset R_k$ is a graph, and the polar equations become a first-order analytic system, solved for the derivative transverse to $N_k$. The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem gives an analytic solution $X$ with data $N_k$.

steps.slogan: Show that the solution $X$ is an integral manifold of $\mathcal I$.
steps.detail: The solution satisfies the polar equations along $X$. The published proof then shows that every form of $\mathcal I$ vanishes on $X$, using that $\mathcal I$ is closed under exterior differentiation and that $N_k$ is already an integral manifold.

steps.slogan: Repeat the step until the dimension reaches $n$.
steps.detail: Choose $R_k$ so that $E_{k+1}$ lies in the tangent space of $R_k$ at $p$; then $N_{k+1} = X$ is tangent to $E_{k+1}$ at $p$. After $n$ steps, $N = N_n$ is an analytic integral manifold through $p$ with $T_pN = E_n = E$.

source.ref: R. L. Bryant, S. S. Chern, R. B. Gardner, H. L. Goldschmidt and P. A. Griffiths, Exterior Differential Systems, MSRI Publications 18, Springer-Verlag, New York, 1991
source.note: The proof of the Cartan-Kahler theorem in chapter III follows the steps above; the original proofs are by E. Cartan and E. Kahler.

concepts.c:analytic-function: Analytic data are what the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem needs.
concepts.c:differential-ideal: Closure of the ideal under $d$ makes the remaining forms vanish on the solution.
concepts.c:exterior-differential-system: The theorem solves the integral manifold problem of such a system.

statement: Four [circles](c:circle) $C_1, \dots, C_4$ touch a circle $K$ at points $A_1, \dots, A_4$ that lie in this order on $K$. Let $t_{ij}$ be the length of a common [tangent](c:tangent-line) of $C_i$ and $C_j$, external if both circles lie on the same side of $K$ and internal if not. Then $t_{12}t_{34} + t_{14}t_{23} = t_{13}t_{24}$.

hypotheses.text: Each circle $C_i$ touches $K$ at a point $A_i$, and the four points are distinct.
The points $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ lie in this cyclic order on $K$.

conclusion: The tangent lengths satisfy $t_{12}t_{34} + t_{14}t_{23} = t_{13}t_{24}$.

proofs.name: Signed radii and Ptolemy
proofs.slogan: Express each tangent length by the chord $A_iA_j$ and the radii, then use Ptolemy's relation for the chords.
proofs.scope: Non-degenerate circles $C_i$; a circle of radius zero gives Ptolemy's theorem itself. A line in place of $K$ is a limit case that is not proved here.

roles.why: Tangency puts the center $O_i$ of $C_i$ on the line $OA_i$ at distance $R - \rho_i$ from the center $O$ of $K$.
The cyclic order makes $A_1A_2A_3A_4$ a convex cyclic quadrilateral, where Ptolemy's relation holds with this pairing.

steps.slogan: Give each circle $C_i$ a signed radius $\rho_i$.
steps.detail: Let $R$ be the radius of $K$ and $O$ its center. Put $\rho_i = r_i$ if $C_i$ lies inside $K$ and $\rho_i = -r_i$ if it lies outside. Tangency puts the center $O_i$ on the ray $OA_i$ with $|OO_i| = R - \rho_i$, so $\angle O_iOO_j = \theta_{ij}$ is the central angle of the [chord](c:chord) $A_iA_j$.

steps.slogan: Compute the tangent length from the law of cosines in triangle $OO_iO_j$.
steps.detail: The law of cosines gives $|O_iO_j|^2 = (R-\rho_i)^2 + (R-\rho_j)^2 - 2(R-\rho_i)(R-\rho_j)\cos\theta_{ij}$. In the three cases (both inside, both outside, one of each), $t_{ij}^2 = |O_iO_j|^2 - (\rho_i - \rho_j)^2$. Expanding gives $t_{ij}^2 = 2(R-\rho_i)(R-\rho_j)(1 - \cos\theta_{ij})$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the tangent length with the chord $A_iA_j$.
steps.detail: Since $1 - \cos\theta_{ij} = 2\sin^2(\theta_{ij}/2)$ and the chord has length $|A_iA_j| = 2R\sin(\theta_{ij}/2)$, taking square roots gives $t_{ij} = \dfrac{|A_iA_j|}{R}\sqrt{(R-\rho_i)(R-\rho_j)}$. The factor under the root depends only on the two circles, not on the angle.

steps.slogan: Multiply Ptolemy's relation for the points $A_i$ by a common factor.
steps.detail: Ptolemy's theorem for the [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral) $A_1A_2A_3A_4$ gives $|A_1A_2||A_3A_4| + |A_1A_4||A_2A_3| = |A_1A_3||A_2A_4|$. By step 3, each product $t_{ij}t_{kl}$ equals the matching chord product times $\sqrt{\prod_{m=1}^{4}(R-\rho_m)}\,/R^2$, the same factor for all three pairings. Multiplying by this factor gives the claim.

source.note: A direct derivation with signed radii; the reduction of Casey's theorem to Ptolemy's theorem through the chords of K is the classical idea.

concepts.c:chord: Each tangent length is proportional to a chord of $K$.
concepts.c:circle: The proof compares four circles with the circle $K$ that they touch.
concepts.c:cyclic-quadrilateral: The tangency points form a cyclic quadrilateral, the setting of Ptolemy's theorem.
concepts.c:tangent-line: The tangent length is the quantity that the relation connects.

statement: Let $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ be [triangles](c:triangle) in the plane. If their three sides match (SSS), or two sides and the included angle match (SAS), or two angles and the included side match (ASA), then a [rigid motion](c:rigid-motion) maps $A, B, C$ to $A', B', C'$.

hypotheses.text: The figures $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are nondegenerate [triangles](c:triangle) in the Euclidean plane.
One criterion holds: SSS, or SAS ($|AB| = |A'B'|$, $|AC| = |A'C'|$, $\angle A = \angle A'$), or ASA ($|AB| = |A'B'|$, $\angle A = \angle A'$, $\angle B = \angle B'$).

conclusion: A composition of translations, rotations and reflections maps $A, B, C$ to $A', B', C'$, so all corresponding sides and angles are equal.

proofs.name: Reduction to SSS
proofs.slogan: Reduce SAS and ASA to SSS by trigonometry, then place the triangles on each other by a rigid motion.
proofs.scope: The three criteria SSS, SAS and ASA. The criteria AAS and RHS follow in the same way and are not proved here.

roles.why: A nondegenerate triangle has noncollinear vertices, so $A' \ne B'$ and the law of sines applies.
The criterion gives $|AB| = |A'B'|$ and, directly or through trigonometry, the other two sides.

steps.slogan: Reduce SAS to SSS with the law of cosines.
steps.detail: The law of cosines gives $|BC|^2 = |AB|^2 + |AC|^2 - 2|AB||AC|\cos A$, and the same formula holds for $B'C'$. The data of SAS are equal, so $|BC| = |B'C'|$ and all three sides match.

steps.slogan: Reduce ASA to SSS with the angle sum and the law of sines.
steps.detail: The angle sum $\pi$ gives $\angle C = \angle C'$. The law of sines gives $|BC| = |AB|\sin A/\sin C$ and $|CA| = |AB|\sin B/\sin C$, and the same for $A'B'C'$. So all three sides match.

steps.slogan: Move $A$ to $A'$ and $B$ to $B'$ by a rigid motion.
steps.detail: Translate $A$ to $A'$, then rotate about $A'$ so that the ray $AB$ becomes the ray $A'B'$; this works because $|AB| = |A'B'|$. Call the composite $\varphi$. It keeps lengths and angles, and $\varphi(A) = A'$, $\varphi(B) = B'$.

steps.slogan: Locate $\varphi(C)$ as a meeting point of two circles.
steps.detail: The point $C'' = \varphi(C)$ has $|A'C''| = |AC| = |A'C'|$ and $|B'C''| = |BC| = |B'C'|$. So $C''$ and $C'$ both lie on the [circle](c:circle) about $A'$ of radius $|AC|$ and on the circle about $B'$ of radius $|BC|$.

steps.slogan: Match $C''$ with $C'$ by a reflection in the line $A'B'$ if needed.
steps.detail: Two circles with distinct centers meet in at most two points, which are mirror images in the line of centers $A'B'$. So $C' = C''$, or $C'$ is the mirror image of $C''$. In the second case compose $\varphi$ with the reflection in $A'B'$, which fixes $A'$ and $B'$.

source.note: The classical criteria (Euclid, Elements I.4, I.8 and I.26), proved here through the law of cosines, the law of sines and a rigid motion.

concepts.c:circle: The third vertex lies on two circles whose centers are known.
concepts.c:rigid-motion: Congruence means that a rigid motion maps one triangle to the other.
concepts.c:triangle: The criteria compare the sides and angles of two triangles.

statement: Let $\varphi$ be a [Hamiltonian diffeomorphism](c:hamiltonian-diffeomorphism) of the standard [symplectic](c:symplectic-manifold) torus $T^{2n} = \mathbb{R}^{2n}/\mathbb{Z}^{2n}$. Then $\varphi$ has at least $2n+1$ [fixed points](c:fixed-point). If all fixed points of $\varphi$ are nondegenerate, then $\varphi$ has at least $2^{2n}$ fixed points.

hypotheses.text: The manifold is the standard [symplectic](c:symplectic-manifold) torus $T^{2n}$ with the form $\sum dx_i \wedge dy_i$.
The map $\varphi$ is the time-one map of a smooth, time-dependent Hamiltonian $H_t$ on $T^{2n}$.
For the second claim, every fixed point of $\varphi$ is nondegenerate.

conclusion: The map $\varphi$ has at least $2n+1$ fixed points, and at least $2^{2n}$ fixed points when all are nondegenerate.

proofs.name: Action functional and Conley index
proofs.slogan: Find fixed points as critical points of the action functional, reduce to finite dimension, and count them by the topology of the torus.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, which rests on Conley's index theory for flows. The count uses 1-periodic orbits that lift to closed loops in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$; the Arnold conjecture for other manifolds is not covered.

roles.why: Periodic variables make the action functional invariant under the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^{2n}$, so the count picks up the topology of the torus.
The Hamiltonian gives the equation whose 1-periodic solutions are the fixed points, and the functional whose critical points they are.
Nondegeneracy makes every critical point nondegenerate, so the Morse inequalities give the sum of the Betti numbers.

steps.slogan: Translate fixed points into periodic solutions of the Hamiltonian equation.
steps.detail: Fixed points of $\varphi$ are initial points of solutions of $\dot x = J\nabla H_t(x)$ that return to the start at time $1$. Lift $H$ to a function on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ that is $\mathbb{Z}^{2n}$-periodic in $x$. Solutions with $x(1) = x(0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ give fixed points, and integer translates of a solution give the same fixed point.

steps.slogan: Write the periodic solutions as critical points of the action functional.
steps.detail: On loops $x\colon S^1 \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ of Sobolev class $H^{1/2}$, the [action functional](c:action-functional) $A_H(x) = \int_0^1 \big(\tfrac12\langle -J\dot x, x\rangle - H_t(x)\big)\,dt$ has the 1-periodic solutions as critical points. It is invariant under $x \mapsto x + k$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}^{2n}$, so it descends to a space over $T^{2n}$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a finite-dimensional gradient flow by Fourier truncation.
steps.detail: Truncate the Fourier series of the loops at order $N$. A priori bounds on periodic solutions give a compact isolated invariant set for the [gradient flow](c:gradient-flow) of the truncated functional on $T^{2n} \times \mathbb{R}^M$, uniformly in $N$.

steps.slogan: Compute the Conley index by deforming $H$ to zero.
steps.detail: The Conley index of the isolated invariant set stays constant under a deformation of $H$ that keeps the a priori bounds. At $H = 0$ the invariant set is a copy of $T^{2n}$, so the index has the cohomology of $T^{2n}$ up to a shift in degree.

steps.slogan: Count the rest points by the cup length and the Betti numbers of the torus.
steps.detail: An isolated invariant set whose index has the [cup product](c:cup-product) structure of $T^{2n}$ contains at least cup length plus one rest points; the cup length of $T^{2n}$ is $2n$, giving $2n+1$. If all rest points are nondegenerate, the Morse inequalities give at least the sum of the [Betti numbers](c:betti-number), $2^{2n}$. Pass to the limit $N \to \infty$.

source.ref: C. C. Conley and E. Zehnder, The Birkhoff-Lewis fixed point theorem and a conjecture of V. I. Arnold, Inventiones Mathematicae 73 (1983), 33-49
source.note: Conley and Zehnder find the periodic solutions as critical points of the action functional by two qualitative statements for flows; the steps above follow that route.

concepts.c:action-functional: Its critical points are the periodic solutions, which are the fixed points.
concepts.c:betti-number: The sum of the Betti numbers of the torus gives the bound $2^{2n}$.
concepts.c:cup-product: The cup length of the torus gives the lower bound $2n+1$.
concepts.c:fixed-point: Fixed points of the map are the objects that the theorem counts.
concepts.c:gradient-flow: The gradient flow of the truncated functional carries the Conley index.
concepts.c:hamiltonian-diffeomorphism: The theorem concerns the time-one map of a Hamiltonian flow.
concepts.c:symplectic-manifold: The torus carries the standard symplectic form that defines the Hamiltonian equation.

statement: A smooth [cubic surface](c:cubic-surface) in the [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb{P}^3$ over an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) contains exactly $27$ lines.

hypotheses.text: The surface $S \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ is the zero set of one homogeneous polynomial $F$ of degree $3$.
The surface $S$ is smooth.
The ground field is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).

proofs.name: Fourth Chern class on the Grassmannian
proofs.slogan: Write the lines as zeros of a section of a rank-4 bundle on a 4-dimensional Grassmannian, show the zeros are simple, and count them by a Chern class.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, over any algebraically closed field. The count is $\int c_4(\mathrm{Sym}^3\mathcal S^\vee) = 27$ and every line is a reduced point of the scheme of lines.

roles.why: Degree $3$ makes the restriction of $F$ to a line a binary cubic, so the bundle has rank $4 = \dim G(2,4)$, and it gives $N_{S/\mathbb{P}^3} = \mathcal O(3)$.
Smoothness makes the normal sequence exact and each line a reduced isolated point of the scheme of lines.
Algebraic closedness makes the points of the zero scheme exactly the lines over the field, so the count is the number of lines.

steps.slogan: Write the lines on $S$ as the zero scheme of a section on the [Grassmannian](c:grassmannian) $G(2,4)$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal S$ be the tautological rank-$2$ subbundle on $G = G(2,4)$, a smooth $4$-fold. Restricting $F$ to each line gives a section $\sigma_F$ of the rank-$4$ bundle $\mathrm{Sym}^3\mathcal S^\vee$. Its zero scheme $Z$ is the scheme of lines in $S$.

steps.slogan: Compute the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle) of a line on the smooth surface.
steps.detail: For a line $L \subset S$, the sequence $0 \to N_{L/S} \to N_{L/\mathbb{P}^3} \to N_{S/\mathbb{P}^3}|_L \to 0$ reads $0 \to N_{L/S} \to \mathcal O(1)^{2} \to \mathcal O(3) \to 0$ on $L \cong \mathbb{P}^1$; it is exact because $S$ is smooth. So $N_{L/S}$ has degree $2 - 3 = -1$, and $N_{L/S} \cong \mathcal O(-1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the zero scheme $Z$ is a finite set of reduced points.
steps.detail: The [tangent space](c:tangent-space) of $Z$ at $[L]$ is $H^0(N_{L/S}) = H^0(\mathcal O_{\mathbb{P}^1}(-1)) = 0$. So every point of $Z$ is isolated and reduced. Since $Z$ is projective, it is a finite set of reduced points, of the expected dimension $4 - 4 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Equate the number of lines with the degree of the fourth [Chern class](c:chern-class).
steps.detail: The zero scheme of a section of a rank-$4$ bundle on a smooth $4$-fold has class $c_4$ when it has dimension $0$. All multiplicities are $1$ by the previous step, so the number of lines is $\int_G c_4(\mathrm{Sym}^3\mathcal S^\vee)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the Chern number with the splitting principle and Schubert calculus.
steps.detail: Let $a, b$ be the Chern roots of $\mathcal S^\vee$. The roots of $\mathrm{Sym}^3\mathcal S^\vee$ are $3a, 2a+b, a+2b, 3b$, so $c_4 = 9ab\,(2(a+b)^2 + ab) = 18\sigma_1^2\sigma_{1,1} + 9\sigma_{1,1}^2$. In $G(2,4)$, $\sigma_1^2\sigma_{1,1} = 1$ and $\sigma_{1,1}^2 = 1$, so $c_4 = 27$.

source.note: The Chern class argument of D. Eisenbud and J. Harris, 3264 and All That, Cambridge University Press, 2016: lines on a cubic surface as zeros of a section of Sym^3 of the dual tautological bundle on G(2,4).

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Every zero of the section is a line defined over the field.
concepts.c:chern-class: The fourth Chern class counts the zeros of the section.
concepts.c:cubic-surface: The lines on this surface are what the theorem counts.
concepts.c:grassmannian: The Grassmannian $G(2,4)$ parametrizes the lines of $\mathbb{P}^3$.
concepts.c:normal-bundle: Its degree $-1$ shows that each line is a reduced isolated point.
concepts.c:projective-space: Lines of the surface are points of the Grassmannian of lines in this space.
concepts.c:tangent-space: The tangent space of the scheme of lines at a line is $H^0$ of its normal bundle.

statement: Let $X$ be a finite set of $v$ points in a [projective plane](c:projective-plane), not all on one line. Then at least $v$ lines contain two or more points of $X$.

hypotheses.text: The set $X$ is a finite set of $v$ points of a [projective plane](c:projective-plane).
The points of $X$ are not all [collinear](c:collinear-points).

conclusion: The number of lines that contain at least two points of $X$ is at least $v$.

proofs.name: Double counting
proofs.slogan: Assume fewer lines than points and count the pairs of a point and a line off it in two ways to reach a contradiction.
proofs.scope: The proof uses only that two distinct points lie on exactly one line, so it holds in every finite linear space. The equality cases (near-pencil and finite projective plane) are not treated.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the counts $b$, $r_p$ and $k_L$ finite, so the sums over points and lines are finite.
It gives at least one pair $(p, L)$ with $p \notin L$ and keeps the denominators $b - r_p$ and $v - k_L$ positive.

steps.slogan: Name the counts $b$, $r_p$ and $k_L$ for the lines that $X$ determines.
steps.detail: Let $b$ be the number of lines with at least two points of $X$. For $p \in X$, let $r_p$ be the number of such lines through $p$. For such a line $L$, let $k_L = |L \cap X|$. Assume for contradiction that $b < v$.

steps.slogan: Show that $r_p \ge k_L$ and that both $r_p < b$ and $k_L < v$ hold.
steps.detail: For $p \notin L$, the $k_L$ lines joining $p$ to the points of $L \cap X$ are distinct, since a line through $p$ and two points of $L$ would be $L$. So $r_p \ge k_L$. If $r_p = b$, every determined line passes through $p$, and then all points of $X$ lie on one line, which is excluded. Also $k_L < v$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\frac{1}{v(b - r_p)}$ with $\frac{1}{b(v - k_L)}$ for every pair with $p \notin L$.
steps.detail: We have $b(v - k_L) - v(b - r_p) = v r_p - b k_L \ge (v - b)k_L > 0$. Both products are positive, so $\dfrac{1}{v(b - r_p)} > \dfrac{1}{b(v - k_L)}$.

steps.slogan: Sum each fraction over all pairs $(p, L)$ with $p \notin L$.
steps.detail: For fixed $p$ there are $b - r_p$ lines $L$ not through $p$, so the first fractions sum to $1/v$ per point and to $1$ in total. For fixed $L$ there are $v - k_L$ points off $L$, so the second fractions sum to $1/b$ per line and to $1$ in total. At least one pair exists.

steps.slogan: Combine the termwise inequality with the two sums to get $1 > 1$.
steps.detail: Termwise, each first fraction exceeds the matching second fraction, so the first total exceeds the second. But both totals equal $1$, which is a contradiction. Hence $b \ge v$.

source.note: The double counting proof in M. Aigner and G. M. Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK, in the chapter on lines in the plane and decompositions of graphs.

concepts.c:collinear-points: The points not being collinear gives a point off a line and bounds the counts.
concepts.c:projective-plane: Two points of the plane lie on exactly one line, which the counts use.

statement: For a closed orientable [surface](c:surface) $S_g$ of [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) $g \ge 1$, the [mapping class group](c:mapping-class-group) $\mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$ is generated by finitely many [Dehn twists](c:dehn-twist) about nonseparating [simple closed curves](c:simple-closed-curve).

hypotheses.text: The surface $S_g$ is closed and orientable of [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) $g \ge 1$.

conclusion: $\mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$ is generated by finitely many Dehn twists about nonseparating simple closed curves.

proofs.name: Action on nonseparating curves
proofs.slogan: Let the mapping class group act on the graph of nonseparating curves and use twists to move between neighbors.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, by induction on the genus: genus $1$ is $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, generated by two twists, and the steps below treat $g \ge 2$. The sharper generating sets of $3g - 1$ (Lickorish) and $2g + 1$ (Humphries) twists are not derived.

roles.why: Cutting along a nonseparating curve lowers the genus, which drives the induction, and genus at least $1$ makes such curves exist.

steps.slogan: Show that the group acts transitively on nonseparating curves.
steps.detail: By the classification of surfaces, the complements of two nonseparating simple closed curves $a$ and $b$ are homeomorphic. So some orientation-preserving homeomorphism takes $a$ to $b$. Hence $\mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$ acts transitively on isotopy classes of nonseparating [simple closed curves](c:simple-closed-curve).

steps.slogan: Join any two nonseparating curves by a chain of nonseparating curves.
steps.detail: For $g \ge 2$, the complex of nonseparating curves, whose edges join curves with disjoint representatives, is connected (Lickorish). So the action is on a connected graph with one vertex orbit.

steps.slogan: Move between neighboring curves by a product of twists.
steps.detail: If two curves $a$ and $c$ meet exactly once, then $T_aT_c(a) = c$ for the [Dehn twists](c:dehn-twist) $T_a$ and $T_c$. Neighboring curves are linked through such an auxiliary curve, so some product of twists about nonseparating curves carries one to the other.

steps.slogan: Reduce the stabilizer of a curve to a surface of lower genus.
steps.detail: Cut $S_g$ along $a$ to get a surface of genus $g - 1$ with two boundary curves. Mapping classes of $S_g$ that fix $a$ come from this cut surface. By induction on the genus, applied to surfaces with boundary, they are products of twists about nonseparating curves.

steps.slogan: Generate the whole group from the stabilizer and the neighbor-carrying elements.
steps.detail: If a group acts on a connected graph with one vertex orbit, it is generated by the stabilizer of a vertex $v$ and any set of elements that carry $v$ to its neighbors. Both parts consist of products of twists, and the stabilizer has finitely many orbits of neighbors, so finitely many twists generate $\mathrm{Mod}(S_g)$.

source.ref: B. Farb and D. Margalit, A Primer on Mapping Class Groups, Princeton Mathematical Series 49, Princeton University Press, 2012, Theorem 4.1 (Dehn-Lickorish)
source.note: Lickorish's proof as presented in chapter 4 of Farb and Margalit; the original is W. B. R. Lickorish, A finite set of generators for the homeotopy group of a 2-manifold, Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 60 (1964), 769-778.

concepts.c:dehn-twist: Dehn twists are the generators and carry curves to neighboring curves.
concepts.c:genus-of-a-surface: Cutting along a nonseparating curve lowers the genus by one.
concepts.c:mapping-class-group: This group is the one that the twists generate.
concepts.c:simple-closed-curve: Twists are taken about nonseparating simple closed curves.
concepts.c:surface: The group is the mapping class group of a closed surface.

statement: Let $N$ be the Gödel-Gentzen [double negation translation](c:double-negation-translation) of propositional formulas. A formula $\varphi$ is derivable from a set $\Gamma$ in [classical logic](c:classical-logic) if and only if $\varphi^N$ is derivable from $\Gamma^N = \{\gamma^N : \gamma \in \Gamma\}$ in [intuitionistic logic](c:intuitionistic-logic).

hypotheses.text: The set $\Gamma$ and the formula $\varphi$ consist of [propositional](c:propositional-logic) formulas built from atoms, $\bot$, $\wedge$, $\vee$ and $\to$, with $\neg A = A \to \bot$.

The translation sends an atom $p$ to $
eg
eg p$, keeps $ ot$, commutes with $\wedge$ and $	o$, and sends $A \vee B$ to $
eg(
eg A^N \wedge 
eg B^N)$.

proofs.name: Induction on formulas and derivations
proofs.slogan: Show that a formula is classically equivalent to its translation, and that translated classical rules are intuitionistically derivable.
proofs.scope: Propositional logic; the first-order case adds $(\forall x A)^N = \forall x A^N$ and $(\exists x A)^N = \neg\forall x\neg A^N$ with one more case per quantifier rule. Glivenko's theorem and the Kolmogorov and Kuroda translations are other members of the family.

roles.why: The formulas are finitely built, so the equivalence and stability lemmas follow by induction on the formula, and the rules are checked one by one.
The clauses of $N$ give the cases of each induction and make every translated formula a conjunction, implication or negation.

steps.slogan: Show that every formula is classically equivalent to its translation.
steps.detail:
By induction on $\varphi$, the formula $\varphi \leftrightarrow \varphi^N$ is a classical tautology. For atoms, $p \leftrightarrow 
eg
eg p$ holds classically; the cases $\wedge$ and $	o$ follow from the induction hypothesis; and $A \vee B \leftrightarrow 
eg(
eg A \wedge 
eg B)$ is De Morgan's law.

steps.detail: Every intuitionistic derivation is a classical one, so $\Gamma^N \vdash_I \varphi^N$ gives $\Gamma^N \vdash_C \varphi^N$. By step 1 each $\gamma \in \Gamma$ classically proves $\gamma^N$, so $\Gamma \vdash_C \varphi^N$, and then $\Gamma \vdash_C \varphi$ by step 1.

steps.detail:
Induct on $\varphi$. The formula $ ot$ is trivial. Atoms and disjunctions translate to negations $

steps.detail:
By induction on derivations, $\Gamma \vdash_C \varphi$ gives $\Gamma^N \vdash_I \varphi^N$. The rules for $\wedge$, $	o$ and $ ot$ translate to themselves. For $\vee$-introduction, $A^N$ and $

source.note: The negative translation of K. Godel and G. Gentzen (1933); the textbook proof is in A. S. Troelstra and D. van Dalen, Constructivism in Mathematics, volume 1, North-Holland, 1988.

concepts.c:classical-logic: One side of the equivalence is derivability in classical logic.
concepts.c:double-negation-translation: The translation embeds classical derivability into intuitionistic derivability.
concepts.c:intuitionistic-logic: The other side is derivability of the translation in intuitionistic logic.
concepts.c:natural-deduction: The proof checks each natural deduction rule after translation.
concepts.c:propositional-logic: The formulas have only connectives, so inductions on formulas apply.

statement: Let $E \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be open and $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ a nonempty open [convex cone](c:convex-cone). Let $f_\pm$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the wedges $W_\pm = \{x \pm iy : x \in E,\ y \in \Gamma,\ |y| < r\}$, continuous up to $E$, with $f_+ = f_-$ on $E$. Then $f_+$ and $f_-$ are restrictions of one holomorphic function on a complex neighborhood of $E$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $W_\pm$ are wedges over an open set $E$ and an open [convex cone](c:convex-cone) $\Gamma$.
The functions $f_+$ and $f_-$ are [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $W_+$ and $W_-$.
Both functions extend continuously to $E$, and the two boundary values agree on $E$.

conclusion: There are an open set $D \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ containing $E$ and a holomorphic function $F$ on $D$ with $F = f_\pm$ on $D \cap W_\pm$.

proofs.name: Gluing across the edge
proofs.slogan: Glue the two functions across the common edge, first in one variable and then in several, and patch the local extensions.
proofs.scope: The continuous version for a convex cone and its opposite; the proof is an outline whose several-variable step rests on the cited work. The cited work also treats distribution boundary values, which is Bogoliubov's original form, and Epstein's generalization.

roles.why: A nonempty open convex cone contains a simplicial subcone that a linear change of variables turns into the orthant, and balls centered on $E$ meet both wedges.
Holomorphy on the wedges is what Morera's theorem and the local extension use, and the identity theorem patches the pieces.
Equal continuous boundary values on $E$ let the two functions join into one continuous function across the edge.

steps.slogan: Shrink the cone to a simplicial cone and change coordinates.
steps.detail: Choose $n$ linearly independent vectors in $\Gamma$. The open cone they span lies in $\Gamma$, and a linear change of variables turns it into the positive orthant. It is enough to extend near each point of $E$ with the smaller wedges, because the final step patches the local pieces.

steps.slogan: Glue the two functions across the edge in one variable.
steps.detail: For $n = 1$, $f_+$ on an upper half-disc and $f_-$ on a lower half-disc have the same continuous values on the diameter. The glued function is continuous on the disc and holomorphic off the diameter, so Morera's theorem makes it holomorphic (Painlevé's theorem).

steps.slogan: Extend across the edge in several variables around each edge point.
steps.detail: After the one-variable case, the cited lectures prove the continuous version by building, in a small polydisc around each point of $E$, a holomorphic function equal to $f_+$ and $f_-$ on the parts of the wedges. For $n = 2$, a shorter proof solves a $\bar\partial$-equation and applies Bochner's theorem on [tube domains](c:tube-domain).

steps.slogan: Patch the local extensions by the identity theorem.
steps.detail: Take balls centered on $E$ whose real parts lie in $E$. Two such balls that meet contain a common real point, hence a common open piece of $W_+$ where both local extensions equal $f_+$. The balls are convex, so the extensions agree on the whole intersection, and they glue to a holomorphic $F$ on the union $D$.

source.ref: W. Rudin, Lectures on the Edge-of-the-Wedge Theorem, CBMS Regional Conference Series in Mathematics 6, American Mathematical Society, Providence, 1971
source.note: Rudin proves the continuous version, from the one-variable case through tubes with a common edge; the theorem is due to N. N. Bogoliubov (1956), with the one-variable case due to Painleve.

concepts.c:convex-cone: The cone fixes the directions in which the wedges lie off the real edge.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The functions on the wedges and the glued function are holomorphic.
concepts.c:tube-domain: Bochner's theorem on tube domains enlarges the domain of a holomorphic function.

statement: For a complex number $s$ that is not an integer, the [digamma function](c:digamma-function) $\psi = \Gamma'/\Gamma$ satisfies $\psi(1-s) = \psi(s) + \pi\cot(\pi s)$.

hypotheses.text: The complex number $s$ is not an integer.

proofs.name: Logarithmic derivative of the reflection formula
proofs.slogan: Take the logarithmic derivative of the reflection formula for the Gamma function at the point $s$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every complex $s$ outside the integers. At integer $s$ the functions $\psi(s)$ or $\psi(1-s)$ are not defined or the cotangent has a pole, so the exclusion is needed.

roles.why: It keeps $s$ and $1-s$ away from the poles of $\Gamma$ and makes $\sin(\pi s)$ nonzero, so every logarithmic derivative below exists.

steps.slogan: Start from the reflection formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z) = \pi/\sin(\pi z)$.
steps.detail: This identity holds for all complex $z$ and is the mathlib lemma Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub. Both sides are functions of $z$, so their logarithmic derivatives agree at every point where both sides are differentiable and nonzero.

steps.slogan: Check that the functions are differentiable and nonzero at $s$.
steps.detail: Since $s$ is not an integer, neither $s$ nor $1-s$ is a pole of $\Gamma$, so $\Gamma$ is differentiable and nonzero at both points. Also $\sin(\pi s) \ne 0$, because $\sin(\pi s) = 0$ only for integer $s$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the logarithm of the left side by the product and chain rules.
steps.detail: The [logarithmic derivative](c:logarithmic-derivative) of a product is the sum of the logarithmic derivatives. The chain rule for $u \mapsto \Gamma(1-u)$ brings a factor $-1$. So the left side has logarithmic derivative $\psi(s) - \psi(1-s)$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the logarithm of the right side by the quotient and chain rules.
steps.detail: The logarithmic derivative of $\pi/\sin(\pi s)$ is minus that of $\sin(\pi s)$, because $\pi$ is constant. The chain rule gives $\pi\cos(\pi s)/\sin(\pi s) = \pi\cot(\pi s)$. So the right side has logarithmic derivative $-\pi\cot(\pi s)$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two logarithmic derivatives and solve for $\psi(1-s)$.
steps.detail: The equation $\psi(s) - \psi(1-s) = -\pi\cot(\pi s)$ rearranges to $\psi(1-s) = \psi(s) + \pi\cot(\pi s)$.

source.note: mathlib applies logDeriv to Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub with logDeriv_fun_mul, logDeriv_fun_div and logDeriv_comp, then unfolds digamma as logDeriv Gamma.

concepts.c:digamma-function: The digamma function is the logarithmic derivative of the Gamma function.
concepts.c:logarithmic-derivative: Logarithmic derivatives turn the product and quotient into sums and differences.

statement: A smooth simple closed curve $C$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with [total curvature](c:total-curvature) $\int_C \kappa\,ds \le 4\pi$ is [unknotted](c:unknot).

hypotheses.text: The curve $C$ is a smooth, regular, simple closed curve in $\mathbb{R}^3$, a [knot](c:knot) or the unknot.
The [total curvature](c:total-curvature) of $C$ is at most $4\pi$.

conclusion: The curve $C$ is isotopic to a round circle, that is, it is [unknotted](c:unknot).

proofs.name: Crofton formula and inscribed polygon
proofs.slogan: Write total curvature as an average count of height maxima, then show that a knotted curve has more than two maxima on a set of directions of positive area.
proofs.scope: The proof shows the contrapositive: a knotted curve has total curvature greater than $4\pi$. The weak inequality $\ge 4\pi$ of Fáry follows from steps 1 to 3, and the strict inequality needs step 4.

roles.why: Smoothness gives the tangent indicatrix for Crofton's formula, and simplicity lets a fine inscribed polygon keep the knot type of $C$.
The bound $\le 4\pi$ is set against the strict lower bound $4\pi$ for knotted curves, which proves the contrapositive.

steps.slogan: Write the total curvature as an average of the number of height maxima.
steps.detail: For a unit vector $e$, let $\mu_C(e)$ count the local maxima of the [height function](c:height-function) $\langle e, \cdot\rangle$ on $C$. Its critical points are the parameters where the tangent $T(s)$ lies on the great circle $e^\perp$. By Crofton's formula on $S^2$, the number $N(e)$ of these parameters satisfies $\int_{S^2} N\,dA = 4\kappa(C)$. For almost every $e$ (Sard), $N(e) = 2\mu_C(e)$. Hence $\kappa(C) = \tfrac12\int_{S^2}\mu_C\,dA$.

steps.slogan: Replace $C$ by a fine inscribed polygon $P$ of the same knot type.
steps.detail: A fine inscribed [polygon](c:polygon) $P$ is isotopic to $C$; merge collinear vertices so that consecutive edges are not parallel. If $v_i$ is a local maximum of the height function on $P$, the arc of $C$ between $v_{i-1}$ and $v_{i+1}$ has a local maximum, and these arcs are disjoint for different maxima. So $\mu_C \ge \mu_P$ almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Show that a knotted polygon has at least two local maxima in almost every direction.
steps.detail: Take $e$ with no horizontal edge and distinct vertex heights. If $\mu_P(e) = 1$, then $P$ has one maximum and one minimum and splits into two arcs that are monotone in height. The horizontal segments joining the two points at each level sweep out an embedded disc bounded by $P$, so $P$ is unknotted. Hence $\mu_P \ge 2$ almost everywhere when $P$ is knotted.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mu_P$ exceeds two on a set of directions of positive area.
steps.detail: Let $u_i$ be the unit edge vectors. At a generic point of the great circle $e \perp u_i$, $\mu_P$ jumps by one exactly when $e\cdot u_{i-1}$ and $e\cdot u_{i+1}$ have the same sign. With no jump for any $i$, every three consecutive edges would be coplanar, so $P$ would be planar and unknotted. So $\mu_P$ takes values $m$ and $m+1$ on open sets, with $m \ge 2$ by step 3.

steps.slogan: Integrate to get $\int\mu_P\,dA > 8\pi$ and conclude.
steps.detail: Let $A > 0$ be the area where $\mu_P \ge 3$. Then $\int\mu_P\,dA \ge 2(4\pi - A) + 3A > 8\pi$. By steps 1 and 2, $\kappa(C) = \tfrac12\int\mu_C\,dA \ge \tfrac12\int\mu_P\,dA > 4\pi$. So a curve with $\kappa(C) \le 4\pi$ is not knotted.

source.note: Milnor's Crofton-type formula and bridge argument (J. Milnor, On the total curvature of knots, Annals of Mathematics 52 (1950), 248-257); the strict inequality is obtained here through an inscribed polygon.

concepts.c:height-function: Counting the maxima of height functions measures the curvature of the curve.
concepts.c:knot: The proof shows that a knot has more than two maxima in a set of directions.
concepts.c:polygon: An inscribed polygon has the knot type of $C$ and a countable structure.
concepts.c:total-curvature: Total curvature is the quantity that Crofton's formula expresses as an average.
concepts.c:unknot: The conclusion is that $C$ is the unknot.

statement: Over a field, every [Lie subalgebra](c:lie-subalgebra) of a [free Lie algebra](c:free-lie-algebra) is a free Lie algebra.

hypotheses.text: The Lie algebra $L$ is a [free Lie algebra](c:free-lie-algebra) on a set $X$ over a field $k$.
The set $M \subseteq L$ is a [Lie subalgebra](c:lie-subalgebra).

conclusion: The subalgebra $M$ is free: some subset of $M$ generates it freely.

proofs.name: Shirshov's lemma and leading terms
proofs.slogan: Choose homogeneous generators for a graded subalgebra, apply Shirshov's lemma, and lift to the general case through top-degree terms.
proofs.scope: Any field and any set of generators, finite or infinite. The proof is an outline in which Shirshov's lemma on independent homogeneous sets is cited.

roles.why: Freeness of $L$ gives the grading by word length and the Lyndon-Shirshov basis on which Shirshov's lemma rests.
The subalgebra $M$ is the object to which the grading, the top-degree terms and the lifting apply.

steps.slogan: State Shirshov's lemma on independent homogeneous sets.
steps.detail: In a free Lie algebra, a set of homogeneous elements such that no element lies in the subalgebra generated by the others freely generates the subalgebra that it generates. Shirshov proves this with Lyndon-Shirshov words and leading terms. It is cited here.

steps.slogan: Choose homogeneous generators of a graded subalgebra degree by degree.
steps.detail: Let $M = \bigoplus_d M_d$ be a graded subalgebra of $L$. In each degree $d$, pick elements of $M_d$ that form a basis modulo the subalgebra generated by $M_1 \oplus \dots \oplus M_{d-1}$. The union $S$ generates $M$ by induction on degree, and no element of $S$ lies in the subalgebra generated by the others.

steps.slogan: Conclude that every graded subalgebra is freely generated by the chosen set.
steps.detail: The set $S$ of step 2 satisfies the hypothesis of the lemma in step 1, so $S$ freely generates $M$. Hence every graded subalgebra of $L$ is free on a homogeneous set.

steps.slogan: Pass from a general subalgebra to the graded subalgebra of its top-degree terms.
steps.detail: For a general subalgebra $M$, let $\mathrm{gr}\,M$ be spanned by the top-degree components of the elements of $M$. It is a graded subalgebra of $L$, because $[\mathrm{top}(a), \mathrm{top}(b)]$ is zero or equals $\mathrm{top}([a,b])$. By step 3, $\mathrm{gr}\,M$ is free on a homogeneous set $\bar S$.

steps.slogan: Lift the free generators of $\mathrm{gr}\,M$ to free generators of $M$.
steps.detail: For each $\bar s \in \bar S$ choose $s \in M$ with top component $\bar s$. By induction on the top degree, the elements $s$ generate $M$: subtract a Lie polynomial in the $s$ with the same top component. A nontrivial relation among the $s$ gives, on top components, one among the free generators $\bar s$, which is impossible.

source.ref: E. Witt, Die Unterringe der freien Lieschen Ringe, Mathematische Zeitschrift 64 (1956), 195-216; A. I. Shirshov, Subalgebras of free Lie algebras, Matematicheskii Sbornik 33 (1953), 441-452
source.note: The key lemma in step 1 is Shirshov's; steps 4 and 5 are the filtration argument that moves freeness from the graded subalgebra of top terms to the subalgebra itself.

concepts.c:free-lie-algebra: The ambient algebra is free, which gives the grading and Shirshov's lemma.
concepts.c:lie-subalgebra: The theorem says that every such subalgebra is itself free.

statement: There are infinitely many [prime numbers](c:prime-number) of the form $a^2 + b^4$ with integers $a$ and $b$.
conclusion: For every $x$ there is a prime $p > x$ with $p = a^2 + b^4$ for some integers $a$ and $b$.

proofs.name: Asymptotic sieve with bilinear forms
proofs.slogan: Count primes among the values $a^2 + b^4$ by a sieve that gives an asymptotic formula, and control its remainder through bilinear forms.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, which gives an asymptotic formula of order $x^{3/4}/\log x$ for these primes up to $x$. The sieve and the estimates for its remainder terms rest on the cited paper.

steps.slogan: Count the representations $n = a^2 + b^4$ as a sequence of weights.
steps.detail: Let $a_n$ be the number of pairs $(a, b)$ with $a^2 + b^4 = n$. Since $a^2 + b^4 = |a + ib^2|^2$ is a norm from the [Gaussian integers](c:gaussian-integer), the sequence has arithmetic structure. The goal is an asymptotic formula for the sum of $a_n$ over primes $n \le x$, of order $x^{3/4}/\log x$.

steps.slogan: Set up the asymptotic sieve for primes.
steps.detail: Friedlander and Iwaniec develop a sieve that detects the primes in the sequence $a_n$ by an asymptotic formula, not only a lower bound. It gets past the parity limit of classical sieves by using bilinear forms, and it needs control of the sieve remainder term.

steps.slogan: Reduce the sieve remainder to a bilinear form.
steps.detail: The remainder term of the sieve involves the distribution of $a_n$ over the multiples of $d$, for many moduli $d$. The paper controls this remainder through a bilinear form in the sieve.

steps.slogan: Estimate the bilinear form by refinements and transformations.
steps.detail: The bilinear [form](c:bilinear-form), a sum over two variables with arbitrary coefficients, is estimated in several stages of refinements and transformations. These stages reduce it to sums that count integer points.

steps.slogan: Count the integer points inside a biquadratic ellipse.
steps.detail: The final input is a count of lattice points in regions bounded by curves $a^2 + b^4 = c$, the biquadratic ellipses. This count and the transformed bilinear form bound the remainder, so the sieve gives the asymptotic formula.

steps.slogan: Deduce that infinitely many primes have the form $a^2 + b^4$.
steps.detail: The asymptotic formula is positive and of order $x^{3/4}/\log x$ for large $x$. So for every $x$ there is a prime $p > x$ of the form $a^2 + b^4$.

source.ref: J. Friedlander and H. Iwaniec, The polynomial X^2+Y^4 captures its primes, Annals of Mathematics 148 (1998), 945-1040
source.note: The paper contains the asymptotic sieve for primes, the estimate of the sieve remainder, the bilinear form in the sieve with its transformations, and the count of points in a biquadratic ellipse.

concepts.c:bilinear-form: The sieve remainder reduces to sums that are bilinear in two coefficient sequences.
concepts.c:gaussian-integer: The value $a^2 + b^4$ is the norm of the Gaussian integer $a + ib^2$.
concepts.c:prime-number: The theorem counts primes among the values of the polynomial.

statement: Let $f_n\colon [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing ([monotone](c:monotone-function)) functions such that the [series](c:series) $\sum f_n(x)$ converges for every $x \in [a,b]$. Then $\sum f_n'(x)$ converges and equals $\big(\sum f_n\big)'(x)$ for every $x$ outside a [null set](c:null-set).

hypotheses.text: Each function $f_n$ is nondecreasing on $[a, b]$.
The series $\sum f_n(x)$ converges for every $x \in [a, b]$.

conclusion: For almost every $x$, the series $\sum f_n'(x)$ converges and equals the derivative of the sum.

proofs.name: Remainders of the series
proofs.slogan: Bound the derivative of each partial sum by the derivative of the total, then apply the bound to fast-shrinking remainders.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Nonnegativity of the functions is only a normalization, and the proof uses Lebesgue's theorem that a monotone function is differentiable almost everywhere.

roles.why: Monotonicity gives differentiability almost everywhere, nonnegative derivatives and the comparison of the derivative of the sum with partial sums.
Convergence at every point makes the sum $F$ and the remainders $r_n$ finite, and lets the remainders be small at $b$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the values at $a$ to make every $f_n$ nonnegative.
steps.detail: Put $g_n = f_n - f_n(a)$. Each $g_n$ is nondecreasing and nonnegative, $\sum g_n(x)$ converges for every $x$ (it converges at $a$ and at $x$), and $g_n' = f_n'$. So assume $f_n \ge 0$. Let $F = \sum f_n$, which is nondecreasing, and $S_n = f_1 + \dots + f_n$.

steps.slogan: Bound the derivative of each partial sum by the derivative of the total.
steps.detail: By Lebesgue's theorem, $F$ and all $f_n$ are differentiable outside a [null set](c:null-set) $Z$. For $x \notin Z$, $F - S_n = \sum_{k>n} f_k$ is nondecreasing, so $S_n'(x) \le F'(x)$. As $f_k' \ge 0$, the series $\sum f_k'(x)$ converges, and its sum is at most $F'(x)$.

steps.slogan: Choose indices so that the remainders $r_n = F - S_n$ are tiny.
steps.detail: Since $\sum f_k(b)$ converges, $r_n(b) \to 0$. Pick $n_1 < n_2 < \dots$ with $r_{n_j}(b) < 2^{-j}$. Each $r_{n_j}$ is nondecreasing and nonnegative, so $0 \le r_{n_j}(x) \le 2^{-j}$ on $[a,b]$, and $\sum_j r_{n_j}(x)$ converges for every $x$.

steps.slogan: Apply the bound to the series of remainders to show that their derivatives tend to zero.
steps.detail: The series $\sum_j r_{n_j}$ has nondecreasing terms and converges everywhere. Step 2 applied to it shows that $\sum_j r_{n_j}'(x)$ converges for almost every $x$, so $r_{n_j}'(x) \to 0$. Since $r_{n_j}' = F' - S_{n_j}'$, we get $S_{n_j}'(x) \to F'(x)$.

steps.slogan: Use monotonicity in $n$ to pass from the subsequence to the whole series.
steps.detail: The partial sums $S_n'(x) = \sum_{k \le n} f_k'(x)$ increase with $n$ because $f_k' \ge 0$. An increasing sequence with a subsequence converging to $F'(x)$ converges to $F'(x)$. So $\sum f_k'(x) = F'(x)$ for almost every $x$.

source.note: The standard proof of Fubini's theorem on differentiation, as in H. L. Royden, Real Analysis, in the chapter on differentiation and integration.

concepts.c:monotone-function: Monotone functions are differentiable almost everywhere with nonnegative derivative.
concepts.c:null-set: The exceptional set where some function is not differentiable is a null set.
concepts.c:series: The theorem is about differentiating a convergent series term by term.
